title: Public-Key Cryptography
subtitle: Key pairs, asymmetric encryption, and the key exchange problem

whyItExists.problem: Symmetric encryption requires both parties to share a secret key. If Alice and Bob have never met, how do they establish that secret? Sending it over the internet means an eavesdropper could intercept it.
whyItExists.solution: Public-key cryptography uses a mathematically linked key pair: anyone can encrypt with the public key, but only the holder of the private key can decrypt. No secret needs to be shared in advance.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Key exchange (Diffie-Hellman, ECDH), digital signatures (RSA-PSS, ECDSA, Ed25519), asymmetric encryption of small data (RSA-OAEP).
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Encrypting large volumes of data (too slow). Instead, use asymmetric crypto to exchange a symmetric key, then switch to AES-GCM.

explainModes.beginner: Imagine a padlock with two modes: anyone can lock it with the public key, but only you can unlock it with your private key. You publish the padlock design; people use it to send you secret messages.
explainModes.simple: Public-key cryptography uses two mathematically linked keys. The public key is shared openly. The private key is kept secret. What one encrypts, only the other can decrypt.
explainModes.standard: Asymmetric cryptography (RSA, ECDH, Ed25519) uses key pairs derived from hard mathematical problems. The public key can be distributed freely. The private key must be kept secure. Asymmetric encryption is slow; in practice it is used only to exchange a symmetric session key.
explainModes.technical: RSA security relies on integer factorisation. ECDH relies on the elliptic curve discrete logarithm. Modern protocols (TLS 1.3, Signal) use ECDH for key agreement (ephemeral keys for forward secrecy) and Ed25519 for signing. Direct RSA encryption with OAEP is rare in modern protocols.
explainModes.deepDive: Public-key infrastructure (PKI) binds public keys to identities using certificates signed by Certificate Authorities. Without PKI, an adversary could substitute their own public key (man-in-the-middle). The Certificate Transparency (CT) log provides an append-only audit trail of all issued certificates.

content.text: Symmetric encryption is fast and secure, but requires sharing a secret key. How do you share that key securely? You can't send it over an insecure channel — that defeats the purpose. Public-key cryptography solves this by allowing parties to establish a shared secret without having communicated privately before.

content.definition: Can be freely distributed to anyone. Used to encrypt data for the owner, or to verify a signature the owner made.
Must remain secret. Used to decrypt data encrypted with the matching public key, or to create a digital signature.
A mathematically linked pair of public and private keys. Data encrypted with one can only be decrypted with the other.

content.text: RSA Key Pair Generation and Encryption

content.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa, padding
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes, serialization
import os

# --- Generate key pair ---
private_key = rsa.generate_private_key(
    public_exponent=65537,
    key_size=2048
)
public_key = private_key.public_key()

# --- Export public key (share this openly) ---
pem_pub = public_key.public_bytes(
    encoding=serialization.Encoding.PEM,
    format=serialization.PublicFormat.SubjectPublicKeyInfo
)
print(pem_pub.decode())  # -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----

# --- Encrypt with public key (anyone can do this) ---
message = b"AES session key: " + os.urandom(32)  # 32-byte session key
ciphertext = public_key.encrypt(
    message,
    padding.OAEP(
        mgf=padding.MGF1(algorithm=hashes.SHA256()),
        algorithm=hashes.SHA256(),
        label=None
    )
)

# --- Decrypt with private key (only you can do this) ---
plaintext = private_key.decrypt(
    ciphertext,
    padding.OAEP(
        mgf=padding.MGF1(algorithm=hashes.SHA256()),
        algorithm=hashes.SHA256(),
        label=None
    )
)
print("Decrypted:", plaintext)

content.text: Never use RSA with PKCS1v15 padding for encryption — it is vulnerable to Bleichenbacher's attack. Always use OAEP padding (RSA-OAEP) for encryption, and PSS padding (RSA-PSS) for signing.

RSA can only encrypt small amounts of data (up to ~190 bytes for a 2048-bit key with OAEP). Real systems use hybrid encryption: use RSA to encrypt a random AES key, then use AES-GCM to encrypt the actual data.

content.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import padding as asym_padding
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
import os

def hybrid_encrypt(public_key, plaintext: bytes) -> dict:
    # 1. Generate a random symmetric session key
    session_key = AESGCM.generate_key(256)
    nonce = os.urandom(12)

    # 2. Encrypt the data with the session key (fast AES)
    aesgcm = AESGCM(session_key)
    ciphertext = aesgcm.encrypt(nonce, plaintext, None)

    # 3. Encrypt the session key with RSA (slow, but only 32 bytes)
    encrypted_key = public_key.encrypt(
        session_key,
        asym_padding.OAEP(
            mgf=asym_padding.MGF1(algorithm=hashes.SHA256()),
            algorithm=hashes.SHA256(),
            label=None
        )
    )
    return {"encrypted_key": encrypted_key, "nonce": nonce, "ciphertext": ciphertext}

# Recipient decrypts the session key with their private key, then decrypts data with AES

a.name: Symmetric (AES-GCM)
a.description: Same key for encryption and decryption
weaknesses: Every pair of parties needs a unique key
a.useWhen: Bulk data encryption (files, database fields, network traffic)

b.name: Asymmetric (RSA, ECDH)
b.description: Public key encrypts; private key decrypts
strengths: Scales to N parties (1 key pair per entity)
weaknesses: RSA limited to ~190 bytes of data
b.useWhen: Key exchange, digital signatures, certificate verification

content.text: In practice, asymmetric cryptography is used only to establish a shared session key. Once both parties have the session key, all further communication uses fast symmetric encryption (AES-GCM).

questions.question: In asymmetric encryption, which key is used to encrypt data?
questions.explanation: The sender uses the recipient's public key to encrypt. Only the recipient's private key can decrypt. The public key can be known by anyone.

questions.question: Why is asymmetric encryption rarely used directly for large files?
options: It produces ciphertext that is too large
It is approximately 1000x slower than symmetric encryption
It requires the recipient to be online
It does not support authenticated encryption
questions.explanation: RSA and ECDH operations are mathematically expensive — orders of magnitude slower than AES. Hybrid encryption uses asymmetric only for key exchange.

questions.question: What is hybrid encryption?
options: Using two different symmetric algorithms together
Using RSA to encrypt a random AES session key, then AES to encrypt the actual data
Combining encryption and digital signatures in one step
Using half the bits for encryption and half for authentication
questions.explanation: Hybrid encryption combines the security of asymmetric cryptography (key distribution) with the speed of symmetric encryption (data encryption).

faq.q: Can asymmetric encryption be used to encrypt large files?
faq.a: No. RSA can encrypt at most ~190 bytes (2048-bit key with OAEP). For large files, use hybrid encryption: RSA encrypts a random AES-256 key, AES-GCM encrypts the file.

faq.q: Is it safe to publish my public key?
faq.a: Yes — that is the whole point. The public key is designed to be shared openly. Security depends entirely on keeping the private key secret.

Giving a copy of a private key to a third party (government, employer) for law enforcement or recovery purposes. It is controversial because it creates a target for attackers and undermines end-to-end encryption.

examples: TLS uses ECDH for key exchange and RSA or ECDSA certificates for server authentication
GPG uses hybrid encryption: RSA encrypts a random AES key, AES encrypts the email body
HTTPS connections start with asymmetric key exchange then switch to symmetric AES for speed
